title: Africa’s green mineral future: when competition becomes self-sabotage
body:
Global demand for Africa’s green minerals is accelerating and suddenly, Africa is “strategic.” However, this has translated neither into stronger African bargaining power nor meaningful structural transformation.

Why? Because too often, African countries negotiate alone.

In fragmented negotiations, power asymmetries dominate. Individual countries—desperate for investment, foreign exchange, or quick wins—offer generous fiscal terms, regulatory concessions, and unrestricted mineral access just to stay “competitive.” But in doing so, they weaken their own leverage and that of their neighbors.

This matters because bargaining power in mineral markets does not come from possession alone—it comes from scale, coordination, and credible alternatives. Our recent report (https://lnkd.in/eyQZNxwP) shows that most green mineral-endowed African countries lack these essential parameters, necessitating a regional coordinated strategy, rather than a purely country-by-country approach, to win in the green mineral race.

When African countries ignore this and act independently:

- Buyers play them off against each other
- Processing and manufacturing commitments are postponed or diluted
- Technology transfer becomes optional, not mandatory
- Industrial learning and capability building are sacrificed for speed

Ultimately, what looks like competition is, in reality, a race to the bottom. This is not how green mineral–led industrialization works.

Fragmentation weakens leverage, raises costs, and ultimately locks Africa into the familiar role of raw material supplier—just in greener clothes.

Africa’s real opportunity lies not in undercutting neighbors, but in bargaining and building together. This means:

- Coordinated regional mineral and industrial strategies
- Shared processing and manufacturing hubs across borders
- Aligned standards, incentives, and trade rules under the AfCFTA
- Collective bargaining with global partners around value addition, not just access

Acting together, African countries can shift from price takers to value makers—and from fragmented suppliers to indispensable players in the global green economy.

The green mineral-led industrialization race will not be won by countries competing against each other for the same investors, offering ever-weaker terms. It will be won by those that coordinate, scale, and bargain as one.

The question is no longer whether Africa has the minerals. It is whether Africa has the political and institutional capacity to stop competing with itself—and start negotiating its future collectively.

Solomon Owusu Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Woubet Kassa, PhD
